curve.note: Local exchange only: Egypt-Byblos timber runs and Cycladic canoes; most of Europe in self-contained Neolithic worlds.
Old Kingdom Egypt trades with the Levant; Early Bronze Anatolian caravan nets; long-distance metal exchange begins.
Assyrian merchants at Kanesh, Minoan palaces rising; eastern tin threads the first true interregional routes.
Palatial world humming: Minoan-Mycenaean sea lanes, Egyptian-Levantine circuits, Baltic amber moving south.
Uluburun-style exchange at its height on paper - but Sea Peoples and systems collapse begin severing the arteries.
Post-collapse dark age: palaces gone, literacy lost, Mediterranean shipping shrunk to coastal hops.
Phoenician colonies from Cyprus to Iberia and the first Greek ventures west restitch the sea.
Persian Royal Road, mature Greek and Punic colonial webs; the Mediterranean rim is one market again.
Hellenistic koine: Alexandria and Rhodes hub a Greek-speaking commercial world from Sicily to Mesopotamia.
Roman conquest links the west, but Cilician pirates and the Mithridatic wars make sailing dangerous.
Pax Romana peak: one currency, 80,000 km of roads, pirate-free grain fleets from Alexandria to Ostia.
Still near peak - but the Antonine Plague travels the very roads and sea lanes that made Rome rich.
Diocletian restores order after the 3rd-century crisis; trade recovers but is more regional, taxed and militarized.
Vandal Africa severs Rome's grain lifeline; Attila's wars; the western sea unravels.
Byzantine ships still bind the eastern Med; Justinian's plague and Lombard wars gnaw at the rest.
Pirenne's nadir: the Med a war frontier between Islam and Byzantium; gold coin and papyrus vanish north of the Alps.
Radhanites and Varangian rivers carry dirhams and silk around a fractured west beset by Viking and Magyar raids.
Recovery: Venice and Amalfi trade with Islam, the Varangian route peaks, new Christian kingdoms open roads.
Commercial revolution: Champagne fairs, crusader ports, Italian fleets - Europe's fairs and towns multiply.
Medieval peak: Pax Mongolica caravans, Hansa kontors and Genoese sea lanes to Flanders knit Eurasia together.
The Black Death rides the trade arteries from Caffa to every port; markets, fairs and fleets stand still.
Recovery under Hansa and Venice, but Ottoman conquest is re-pricing the eastern routes.
Atlantic opening: Antwerp booms, American silver floods in; corsair war makes the Med itself dangerous.
Dutch shipping supreme, but the Thirty Years' War has gutted Germany and mercantilist walls rise.
Age-of-sail globalization: Atlantic circuits, Baltic convoys, the Levant trade - all under mercantilist rules.
Congress peace opens a century of relatively free movement; Britain's navy keeps the sea lanes.
First globalization surging: railways, telegraph, Suez (1869), the gold standard, Cobden-Chevalier free trade.
Peak first globalization: trade near 30% of world GDP, passport-free travel across most of Europe.
Blockade, trench lines and collapsed empires; the continental economy in ruins.
1920s rebuilding restored trade volumes, but new tariff walls between successor states cap it - then the Crash.
Autarkic blocs at war: occupied Europe, blockade and U-boats; movement now means armies and deportations.
The Iron Curtain splits the continent; Marshall aid and the payments union restart the western half.
EEC customs union complete (1968), jet travel and container ships - but half of Europe sits behind the Wall.
The Curtain lifts: borders open eastward, the single market is in sight, Germany reunifies.
Schengen stretches to the Baltic and Poland; the EU-27 single market - the freest movement Europe has ever known.
Migration crisis brings back spot checks; Crimea sanctions cut eastern links; peak connectivity slightly dented.
War walls off Russia; yet Schengen endures and grows (Romania & Bulgaria join fully 2025) - the west stays open.

famousBorders.name: Portugal-Spain (Treaty of Alcanices)
famousBorders.note: Europe's oldest near-unchanged border (1,234 km), set 1297. Sole dispute: Olivenza, held by Spain since 1801.

famousBorders.name: Anglo-Scottish border (Treaty of York)
famousBorders.note: Fixed 1237; only Berwick (1482) and the Debatable Lands (1552) moved since. Internal UK line after 1707.

famousBorders.name: France-Spain (Treaty of the Pyrenees)
famousBorders.note: Crest-line border of 1659, demarcated by the Bayonne treaties 1856-68; leaves Llivia as a Spanish exclave.

famousBorders.name: Norway-Russia (Treaty of Novgorod)
famousBorders.note: 1326 peace set Arctic tribute zones; the exact line was drawn 1826. Today NATO's oldest quiet frontier with Russia.

famousBorders.name: Andorra (Pareage of 1278)
famousBorders.note: Feudal charter split sovereignty between Foix and Urgell; the valleys' borders have not moved since.

famousBorders.name: San Marino
famousBorders.note: Republic by legend since 301 CE; borders unchanged since the 1463 enlargement - the world's oldest state line.

famousBorders.name: Swiss frontiers (Congress of Vienna)
famousBorders.note: Borders and perpetual neutrality fixed 1815; untouched by two world wars.

famousBorders.name: Rhine-Danube Roman limes
famousBorders.note: Rome's river frontier for four centuries; its ghost lingers in later borders, dialects and the wine-beer line.

famousBorders.name: Eider line (Denmark-Empire)
famousBorders.note: The Treaty of Heiligen made the Eider Denmark's southern edge for a millennium, until the 1864 war.

famousBorders.name: Offa's Dyke (England-Wales)
famousBorders.note: Mercian earthwork of c. 785 still shadows the modern English-Welsh boundary.

famousBorders.name: Ottoman-Habsburg Military Frontier
famousBorders.note: Fortified soldier-settler cordon (Militaergrenze) guarding the Habsburg south against the Ottomans for 350 years.

famousBorders.name: Oder-Neisse line (Germany-Poland)
famousBorders.note: Drawn at Potsdam 1945; Germany renounced the lands beyond it, with final recognition in the 1990 treaty.

famousBorders.name: Curzon line (Poland's eastern border)
famousBorders.note: Proposed 1919, imposed at Yalta/Potsdam 1945; now the EU-Schengen edge facing Belarus and Ukraine.

famousBorders.name: Green Line, Cyprus
famousBorders.note: UN buffer zone along the August 1974 ceasefire; 180 km slicing the island - and Nicosia - in two.

tradeSystems.name: Bronze Age tin, copper & amber routes
tradeSystems.note: Palace-to-palace circuits: Cypriot copper, eastern tin, Baltic amber; the Uluburun wreck carried goods of seven cultures.

tradeSystems.name: Phoenician maritime network
tradeSystems.note: Tyre and Sidon strung colonies from Cyprus to Gadir; Tartessian silver flowed east past Carthage.

tradeSystems.name: Greek colonial network
tradeSystems.note: Hundreds of poleis from Massalia to Crimea traded grain, wine, oil and ideas across a Greek-speaking sea.

tradeSystems.name: Persian Royal Road
tradeSystems.note: 2,700 km of posting stations from Sardis toward Susa; royal couriers in a week, caravans in three months.

tradeSystems.name: Hellenistic grain & luxury circuit
tradeSystems.note: Alexandria, Rhodes and Delos hubbed a koine-Greek market binding Egypt, Syria and the Aegean.

tradeSystems.name: Roman Mare Nostrum
tradeSystems.note: Grain fleets, 80,000 km of roads and a pirate-free sea: the ancient world's connectivity peak under the Pax Romana.

tradeSystems.name: Radhanite network
tradeSystems.note: Jewish merchants bridged Christendom and Islam from the Rhone to Cathay - furs and swords east, silk and spice west.

tradeSystems.name: Varangian river routes
tradeSystems.note: Norse-Rus portages linked the Baltic to Byzantium and the Caliphate; Arab dirhams piled up in Swedish hoards.

tradeSystems.name: Venice & Genoa galley empires
tradeSystems.note: Rival sea empires: Venice ruled the Levant runs, Genoa the Black Sea; both opened sea lanes to Flanders after 1277.

tradeSystems.name: Champagne fairs
tradeSystems.note: A six-fair annual cycle where Flemish cloth met Italian silver and Levant spices - medieval Europe's clearing house.

tradeSystems.name: Hanseatic League
tradeSystems.note: Luebeck-led league of ~200 towns; kontors at Novgorod, Bergen, Bruges and London moved fur, fish, wax and grain.

tradeSystems.name: Pax Mongolica Silk Road
tradeSystems.note: 'The road to Cathay is perfectly safe, day or night' - Pegolotti. Caffa and Tana funneled Asia into Genoese holds.

tradeSystems.name: Dutch entrepot & Baltic 'mother trade'
tradeSystems.note: Fluyts hauled Danzig grain and Norway timber to Amsterdam, redistributing south for salt, wine and silver.

tradeSystems.name: Levant companies (English & French)
tradeSystems.note: Marseille and London ran cloth-for-silk exchanges with Smyrna, Aleppo and Alexandria under Ottoman capitulations.

tradeSystems.name: Atlantic age of sail (London hub)
tradeSystems.note: London eclipsed Amsterdam; colonial sugar and cotton met Baltic stores and Iberian wine - ocean legs leave the map.

tradeSystems.name: Steam, rail & Suez (first globalization)
tradeSystems.note: Steamships through Suez (1869), railways and telegraphs drove trade to ~30% of world GDP by 1913.

tradeSystems.name: COMECON bloc trade
tradeSystems.note: Commerce re-routed behind the Iron Curtain: Moscow-centered barter of oil, machinery and grain among socialist states.

tradeSystems.name: EU single market & Schengen
tradeSystems.note: Free movement of goods, people, capital and services since 1993; passport-free Schengen from 1995 - history's peak.
